summary: A summary listing of the RFCs numbered 2100 through 2199. It is an informational index to help readers see what was published in that range, not a technical specification.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a table of contents for one hundred of the Internet's rulebooks, so you can see which ones exist.

subtitle: A guide to the 100 RFCs published in the 2100–2199 range.

tldr.problem: Readers need a way to see what RFCs exist in a given number range and get a quick sense of what each one is about without reading the full texts.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2199 provides a brief annotated list of all 100 RFCs from RFC 2100 through RFC 2199, with one or two sentences describing each. RFCs on the standards track are marked, and the document notes that readers should check the latest RFC standards guide for current status.
tldr.outcome: This document serves as a table of contents and discovery tool for RFCs in the 2100s range. Later ranges have similar summary RFCs (e.g., RFC 3000 for 3000–3099).

facts.label: Purpose
facts.value: Navigation and discovery of RFCs in the range

today: RFC 2199 is an informational RFC, part of a historical series of summary documents. It is no longer updated; the RFC library has since moved well beyond the 2100–2199 range. Later RFC ranges have their own summary documents. RFC 2199 and similar summaries serve as historical snapshots of what Internet technologies were in development during 1997–1998.

sections.title: What Is This Document?
sections.content:
RFC 2199 is a summary of the RFCs numbered 2100 through 2199. It is one of a series of periodic summary RFCs that list all RFCs in a given numeric range, provide a short title and description for each, and note which ones are on the IETF standards track.

This type of summary RFC serves as both a table of contents and a discovery tool. When someone wonders what RFCs exist in a particular range, they can consult the summary. The document does not define any protocol or standard itself; it is purely informational and is intended to help readers navigate the growing RFC library.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a big list that says "here are all the rulebooks from 2100 to 2199, and here is one sentence about each one."

sections.title: What the 2100s Cover
sections.content:
The RFCs in the 2100–2199 range, published mostly in 1997 and early 1998, cover a wide array of Internet technologies. Notable examples in this range include:

  • Transport and protocols: RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) payload formats for audio and video, TCP pipelining extensions for SMTP, UDP protocol definitions.
  • Multicast: MARS (multicast over ATM), VENUS (a hypothetical multicast extension), and CBT (Core Based Trees) multicast routing.
  • Naming and addressing: DNS clarifications and extensions, IMAP URL schemes, domain name system security.
  • Email and messaging: IMAP4 improvements, SMTP extensions, mailbox referrals, authentication methods.
  • Caching: Internet Cache Protocol (ICP) and web caching applications.
  • Operations and security: Site security handbook, roaming implementations, IPv6 routing transitions.

The document notes that the RFCs listed cover both standards-track proposals (on their way to becoming standards) and informational memos (like this one) that provide information without seeking standards approval.
sections.plainLanguage: These RFCs are about things like how to send video over the Internet, how to make email faster, how to find computers by name, and how to keep networks secure.

sections.title: Standards Track vs. Informational
sections.content:
The RFC 2199 summary marks RFCs with [STANDARDS-TRACK] to indicate that they are on the IETF standards track, meaning they are part of the formal process to become Internet standards. Many RFCs in the 2100–2199 range are marked this way.

Other RFCs are purely informational. These include vendor specifications (like RFC 2188 on ESRO), thought experiments exploring problems (like RFC 2191 on VENUS), security guides, reviews of existing implementations, and historical references. Informational RFCs can be valuable even though they are not pursuing standards status.

RFC 2199 itself is informational. The memo notes that readers should consult the latest edition of "Internet Official Protocol Standards" for the current status of RFCs, since standards-track RFCs may change status over time as the IETF reviews and refines them.
sections.plainLanguage: Some rulebooks are on their way to becoming official standards. Others are just information to help everyone understand what is going on. This one is just information.

sections.title: Using This Summary as a Discovery Tool
sections.content:
RFC summary documents like RFC 2199 are primarily useful for discovery and navigation. If you are researching a particular topic (e.g., multicast, DNS, IMAP), you can scan through the summaries to find related RFCs in a range, then read the full RFCs that interest you. The one-sentence descriptions give just enough information to decide whether to read further.

Because RFCs are numbered sequentially by publication date (with new numbers assigned as each RFC is published), the numbers themselves carry historical information: RFCs 2100–2199 are all roughly from 1997–1998. Reading the summaries for a given range gives a snapshot of what Internet technologies were being discussed at that time.

Similar summary RFCs exist for other ranges: RFC 3000 summarizes RFC 3000–3099, RFC 4000 summarizes RFC 4000–4099, and so on. Together, they form a navigational structure for the entire RFC library.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want to know what people were working on around 1997, you can read this summary. If you need to find an RFC about a specific topic, you can scan the summaries for keywords and then read the full ones.
